extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: A dataset of narrative passages for evaluating word prediction requiring broad discourse context, where humans can guess the last word from the whole passage but not from the last sentence alone.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, German Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernandez
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Passages were sourced from the Book Corpus, split by novel into training and development/testing partitions, automatically filtered using language models to remove locally guessable items, and then evaluated by human subjects in a three-step CrowdFlower pipeline to retain passages whose target word was guessable from the full passage but not from the target sentence alone.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Unpublished novels from the Book Corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The source corpus was deduplicated and filtered for offensive material; novels were randomly partitioned; passages easy for standard language models were excluded using a probability threshold; final dataset items were selected only if two subjects guessed the target from the full passage and none of up to ten subjects could guess it from the target sentence alone.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Each passage was constructed as a context plus a target sentence, where the context was the minimum number of complete preceding sentences containing at least 50 tokens; duplicate removal and offensive-material filtering were applied to the source corpus; automated filtering removed passages easy for language models.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects on CrowdFlower guessed the target word in a three-step protocol: one subject guessed from the whole passage; if correct, a second subject guessed from the whole passage; if also correct, additional subjects guessed from the target sentence only until the word was guessed or ten unsuccessful guesses were reached. Items were kept only if two full-passage guesses were correct and no sentence-only subject guessed the word. Subjects in step 3 were allowed three guesses per sentence.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors used strict exact-match inclusion criteria, requiring two consecutive correct whole-passage guesses and zero successful sentence-only guesses out of up to ten subjects; they also analyzed discard rates across annotation steps and noted cost constraints affecting the number of annotators.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 2 full-passage annotations, plus up to 10 sentence-only annotations
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A pre-trained recurrent neural network, a standard 4-gram model, a recurrent neural network, and a feed-forward model
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set and training corpus were released for download, and the test set was planned for release at the time of a public competition.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to stimulate development of language models that genuinely capture non-local phenomena and broad-context understanding in natural language.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Proper nouns are heavily overrepresented in the dataset, and direct speech appears more often than in the input data; the dataset also often contains target words already present in the context.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset construction is costly and uses strict exact-match criteria that may exclude plausible synonymous continuations; cost constraints prevented using more annotators at stage 1; standard language models are also designed to fail on the benchmark because early filtering removed passages they could predict.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: A benchmark and challenging test set for evaluating language models on broad-context word prediction; the training partition is intended for training models on raw text, and the development data can be used to fine-tune models to LAMBADA-specific passages.

name.evidence: In this paper, we introduce the LAMBADA dataset (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects).

description.evidence: We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. LAMBADA is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word.

url.evidence: The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, can be downloaded at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/ .

inLanguage.evidence: The task is to guess the last word of the target sentence (the target word). The constraint that the target word be the last word of the sentence, while not necessary for our research goal, makes the task more natural for human subjects.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). We randomly divided the novels into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. To reduce time and cost of dataset collection, we filtered out passages that are relatively easy for standard language models... A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps.

Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded. rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The fact that it contains unpublished novels minimizes the potential usefulness of general world knowledge and external resources for the task... The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list... We randomly divided the novels into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions... Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded... if no subject was able to guess the target word, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: LAMBADA consists of passages composed of a context (on average 4.6 sentences) and a target sentence. The context size is the minimum number of complete sentences before the target sentence such that they cumulatively contain at least 50 tokens... The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list... Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps. For a given passage, 1. one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage... 2. a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage... 3. more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10; if no subject was able to guess the target word, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset. The subjects in step 3 were allowed 3 guesses per sentence.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84–86% items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2 and another 3–5% at step 3... Note that the criteria for passage inclusion were very strict: We required two consecutive subjects to exactly match the missing word, and we made sure that no subject (out of ten) was able to provide it based on local context only, even when given 3 guesses.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: 1. one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage... 2. a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage... 3. more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: LAMBADA proposes a word prediction task where the target item is difficult to guess (for English speakers) when only the sentence in which it appears is available

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: We used a combination of four language models, chosen by availability and/or ease of training: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2011) and three models trained on the Book Corpus (a standard 4-gram model, a RNN and a feed-forward model; see SM for details... ). Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: To promote research in this direction, we plan to announce a public competition based on the LAMBADA data. The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, can be downloaded at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/ . The test set will be made available at the time of the competition.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: We thus propose LAMBADA as a challenging test set, meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text. We hope the computational community will be stimulated to develop novel language models that are genuinely capturing the non-local phenomena that LAMBADA reflects.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Figure 2(b) shows that most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%)... In fact, proper nouns are hugely overrepresented in LAMBADA... More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context... As a final observation, intriguingly, the LAMBADA items contain (quoted) direct speech significantly more often than the input items overall (71% of LAMBADA items vs. 61% of items in the input sample)

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Overall, each item in the resulting dataset costed $1.24 on average... Cost considerations also precluded us from using more subjects at stage 1... An alternative to this perfect-match approach would have been to include passages where broad-context subjects provided other plausible or synonymous continuations. However, it is very challenging... For this reason we went for the strict hit-or-miss approach... We also note that, because of the way we have constructed LAMBADA, standard language models are bound to fail on it by design

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We thus propose LAMBADA as a challenging test set, meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text. We built the LAMBADA dataset from the latter, with the idea that models tackling LAMBADA should be trained on raw text from the training partition... The development data can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of the LAMBADA passages.
